en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Prince Mupō, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In a former life, I was the crown prince of the King of Vārāṇasī, named Mupò;..."
From the moment of his birth, he was extraordinary; his countenance was upright and handsome, peerless and without equal.

He possessed the knowledge of his own past lives, including events from incalculable kalpas, the good and evil he had encountered, the retributions for his sins and merits, and whether his life was long or short, beautiful or ugly.
He fully perceived and knew all things: passing away from this life and being born in that, and the origins from which he had come to be born.
At the age of thirteen, he remained silent with his mouth closed. "The King has only this one son;
all the people of the kingdom hold him in great affection, for he was destined to succeed the lineage and inherit the royal throne.

However, because he possesses the recollection of his past lives and understands the calamities and blessings, as well as the survival and extinction, of billions of years, he maintains silence until the age of thirteen. He has cast aside his physical form, setting his will upon the void. Drifting and unspeaking, he is indifferent to hunger and cold; his simplicity is like that of a withered tree—though he possesses ears and eyes, he does not attend to seeing or hearing."
Though his wisdom and discernment are far-reaching, he is as if without conscious intent;
he does not fear defilement or disgrace, nor does he harbor hatred or affection;
like one who is blind or deaf, he speaks neither of the west nor of the east.
He appeared as if blind and deaf, unlike other men.
His father, the King, was filled with anxiety and great distress; he felt deep shame before his neighboring states, fearing they would look down upon and mock him.
He summoned the brahmins of the kingdom and questioned them:
"For what reason is this child unable to speak?
The brahmins looked at one another and said:
"This child is an evil man; although his countenance is upright and exceptionally handsome, he harbors malice within.
Observing his silent demeanor, he intends to harm his parents and bring ruin upon the state and the lineage before long; he must not be raised."
Since he cannot speak, what benefit could he possibly bring to the King?
That the King now has no further sons at all is entirely due to the obstruction and firm resistance of this wicked son; it is he who has caused Your Majesty not to have more offspring.
"Your Majesty should abandon him and bury him alive;
only then can Your Majesty's person be preserved, the state protected, and the lineage secured, after which you shall again obtain a noble son.
Otherwise, there will be great peril!"
The king, believing the madman’s delusion to be the truth, was immediately overcome with grief and anxiety;
he could find no peace whether sitting or rising, ceased to enjoy music and dance, and found no pleasure in fine garments or delicacies.
He then deliberated with the elders and ministers, saying: "What should be done?
There was a minister who said:
"Let us cast him far away into the deep mountains, a place where no people dwell."
Some ministers said, "Cast him into deep water.
Another minister said, "We should follow the master's words;
however, let us construct a deep pit with side-entrances like chambers, provide him with provisions and attend him with five servants, and place him alive within it."
"Following what the command dictates, it is an act of empty and futile destruction.
The king immediately followed these words of his minister; that very morning he dispatched a servant to go out and bury [the child] alive.
The Crown Prince felt deep sorrow within his heart; he lamented their ignorance and delusion with immeasurable compassion.
His mother, filled with pity and grief, her heart broken with pain, said:
"I have given birth to one who lacks auspicious marks; my meager fortune has brought me this calamity, which cuts through my very bowels."
Choking with sobs and weeping tears, his sorrowful heart uttered indistinct moans; his longing and attachment were beyond remedy.
Having no choice in the matter, he resigned himself to letting go, sent someone to carry it out, and intended to bury it and cast it away.
They took all of the crown prince’s garments, robes, necklaces, and jewels, and sent them all away.
Furthermore, they ordered that outside, all his garments and jewels be stripped off and set aside in one place, and then they dug a pit together.
Before the pit was finished, Mupò (Mūkapāla) remained alone upon his cart, reflecting deeply within himself, speaking thus with his own mind:
"From the King downward to the common people, everyone says of me that I am truly deaf, foolish, and mute, unable to speak.

The reason I do not speak is precisely because I wish to abandon worldly entanglements, settle my body, avoid affliction, and deliver my spirit from suffering. Yet now, I am instead endangered by this deception."
Once their lives had ended and they had fallen into that pit, those people remained silent and took the clothing, coverlets, and jewels for themselves.
The group of men who had dug the pit were unaware as the spirits took the goods and departed.
At that time, Mupai went to the water’s edge, purified himself by bathing, anointed his body with fragrances, and put on all his garments and ornaments;
arriving at the pit, he asked, "For what purpose was this pit made?"
The servant replied, "The king has a son named Mupai, who is mute, deaf, and mentally deficient; he is thirteen years old and cannot speak."
The king questioned the brahmin, and the brahmin’s teacher replied:
"You must bury him alive; only then will you be secure and at peace, the state will flourish, and your lineage will be honored, bringing benefit to your future descendants. It is for this reason."
"We have dug a pit, intending to bury Mupò.
Mupò then said, "I am indeed Prince Mupò."
The people were immediately struck with terror, their hair standing on end; they ran toward him and looked upon the chariot, but Mupò was nowhere to be seen.
Returning to the site of the pit, they observed it closely and listened for sounds, yet there was a completely different noise, its radiance like that of the moon—a thing rarely heard in the world.
Those walking stopped, and those sitting rose; birds and beasts alike gathered together, prostrating before the Prince to listen to his words.
Mupo said again: "Observe my hands and feet;
examine my appearance. Why have you, all deluded and deceived by falsehoods, mistaken error for truth and abandoned one another?"

The words he uttered upon forming this intention were composed into elegant prose; those to his left and right were filled with awe and reverence, and all present were moved to profound humility. From the highest to the lowest, there was none who did not submit and follow him.

Their demeanor was one of great alarm; they were restless and trembling with fear. Looking at one another in pairs, their faces turned pale blue, and they all said, "The Prince is truly divine; he is indeed like this!"
They all stepped forward to pay their respects, bowing their heads in supplication:
"We pray that you will pardon our offenses and allow us to return together to the palace to reach our father, the King. Mupò said:
"Now that I have been cast out, it is not fitting for me to return.
You should go directly and inform the King so that he may know.
The servant then galloped away and reported this to the King accordingly.
His mother was filled with grief and sent someone to inquire about the circumstances.

The servant said, "The Crown Prince is most extraordinary; the moment he opens his mouth to speak, it truly strikes terror into people. Those who hear him are all agitated, and those who travel fill the roads."
The King was struck with astonishment; filled with both joy and sorrow, he marveled deeply at the reason for this.
The King and his consort then mounted the carriage together to go and welcome the Prince;
the people of the kingdom, both old and young, all rushed forth, and the roads were crowded with those who came to gaze upon him.
They all said,
"The Crown Prince seems as though he wishes to see the divine form.
Before the King had even arrived, Mupò’s mind thought to itself:
"I shall study the Way; let me just give rise to this intention.
As soon as he had spoken these words, Śakra Devendra immediately manifested for him a pleasure garden with bathing pools and various fruit-bearing trees, its delights beyond compare.
Mupo immediately cast off the fine clothes and precious jewels upon his body and transformed into a practitioner; his robes were solemn and dignified.
Just as the king was about to arrive, he encountered Mupo sitting beneath a tree.
When Mupò saw that the King had arrived, he immediately rose to meet him, and the King paid his respects to him.
Mupò then said,
"Great King, please be seated."

When the king heard the voice and speech of Mopao, and witnessed his majestic spiritual radiance shaking heaven and earth—unparalleled and peerless—he was filled with great joy and immediately informed Mopao:
"Let us return together to the kingdom; you shall occupy the throne and govern the administration, while I request to step aside."
Mupò said: "No, no!
It is because I fear and loathe the diligent suffering of hell, with its myriad forms of grief and poison."

In the past, I once served as the king of this country, named Susīma. I governed the realm with the True Dharma and practiced all manner of goodness; for twenty-five years, the use of whips and staves was not employed, weapons of war were not maintained, and there were no prisoners in the jails.
He practiced generous giving and benevolent love; his kindness flowed forth and his virtue spread abroad as he rescued and relieved the poor and destitute, without any greed or stinginess.
Yet, despite these deeds, he still committed minor transgressions and ultimately fell into hell for more than sixty thousand years.
There he was steamed, boiled, flayed, and torn apart; the agony was so cruel it was unbearable, such that he could not seek death nor could he find life.
At that time, wherever their parents may be, though they possess immeasurable wealth numbering in the billions, being both rich and noble, their happiness shall be boundless.
"Could you possibly know that I am there, undergoing such severe torture in hell?
Could you possibly come back to share in the suffering of my body? "No."
"What is the reason for my falling into this transgression?
In the past, when I was a great king, all the subordinate territories and vassal states were under my dominion."

The king was by nature compassionate and benevolent; his virtue was exceedingly pure, and his laws were not strict. Consequently, the various minor kings all treated him with contempt and ease, and they deliberated together:
"Now this Great King is cautious, kind, and weak; his majesty and prohibitions do not restrain us, and his virtue is insufficient to govern a great kingdom.
We must join forces to attack and depose him."
They immediately raised their armies and came to attack the great kingdom.

King Susīma, however, met them by bestowing upon them rare treasures and precious goods; he further pacified and consoled them with high offices and generous stipends, enticing them to settle there in peace.
They immediately ceased their hostilities and each returned to their own country.
Not long after this, they came again to attack and wage war, not just once but repeatedly.
The ministers of the great kingdom were all filled with indignation and reported to the Great King:
"The various minor states are foolish and ignorant, devoid of righteousness; they disregard the gravity of their transgressions and repeatedly commit acts of insolence.
They have fostered rebellion and offended their superiors, causing the people to flee in turmoil and keeping the state in a state of constant alert."
"You ought to execute them in order to eliminate this scourge.
The King said, "As the parents of the people, I must strive for benevolent transformation; I shall exercise self-compassion in nurturing all things and risk my own life to save the multitude."
"He is still like an infant; pitying his lack of discernment, I shall guide him gradually and cannot bear to inflict harm upon him.
The King harbored great compassion, universally grieving for all living beings, and forever abandoned any intention of slaughter.

The ministers, unable to endure being repeatedly humiliated and treated with contempt by the subordinate cities and small states, acted out of indignation regardless of the danger; they secretly raised private armies to attack various kingdoms, resulting in the mass slaughter of the people.

"When the Great King heard this, he was deeply moved by grief and shed tears like rain; for all the deceased people of the various kingdoms, he observed mourning as if they were his own sons, his compassion being boundless."
When the various minor kings saw that the great king possessed such compassionate concern for his people, they all immediately submitted and came to seek refuge under him.

As for those who came to seek refuge, the great king would provide them with meals, and the high officials would prepare the food; in all cases, it was necessary to slaughter oxen, sheep, and other livestock to provide the various flavors.
Whenever it was time for slaughter, he would invariably first announce it.
Although the King’s heart was compassionate, as there was no other recourse, he would nod his head in consent.
It is because of this that he incurred this offense and undergoes such diligent suffering.
Every time I reflect upon this, my heart is filled with profound dread; my hair stands on end, and my body breaks into cold sweat.

The reason I have remained silent is that I recall the various fortunes and misfortunes, safety and peril, successes and failures experienced throughout my past lives, fearing that I might encounter them again. Therefore, I have kept my tongue tied and remained speechless until the age of thirteen, hoping that through stillness and silence I might avoid blemish and escape defilement, transcend worldly toil, bid eternal farewell to the mundane world, and never again meet with calamity.

I further thought that I wished to close my mouth and remain silent, yet I would be buried alive by the King; I feared that at a later time, the King might again suffer this calamity, and once having entered hell, there would be no time of release.
It was not my intention to cause the King to incur guilt, which is why I spoke again.
I merely wish to pursue the Way and maintain a mind of non-action; I do not delight in being a king.
Human beings dwelling in this world are as fleeting and illusory as a dream; the joys and pleasures of family life last but a moment.
Calculating the span of life, it is but brief, yet anxieties and fears are prolonged; there is little pleasure and much suffering, with myriad forms of affliction.
Therefore, the wise regard a kingdom, wealth, and loved ones as burdens, and manifold desires as dust.

If I were to become king, I would surely again succumb to arrogance and dissipation, greedily seeking pleasure and causing the people distress and anxiety, becoming a source of great calamity for the world.
Therefore, wishing to eliminate sorrow and cast off worldly entanglements, one should reverse the flow of existence to seek its source and rescue those who have not yet crossed over.

Life in this world is like a temporary lodging; there is not a single thing upon which one can rely. As years pass and time shifts, life grows frail and the end approaches swiftly; one cannot linger or delay, for one drifts further and further from the Way day by day.
Not coveting wealth or nobility, nor valuing precious treasures, he cast aside worldly glory, contemplated the Great Way, soared aloft and traveled afar, thereby liberating himself from the world.
The father king said: "How could this be?
You are a wise man; you ought to have been lenient regarding my shortcomings rather than simply abandoning me like this."
The king’s heart was filled with both sorrow and joy as he deeply repented for his actions.
The prince spoke again:
"How have I ever heard of a father and son being born only to abandon one another?"
Our affection has already been estranged and our kinship severed; as you have committed transgressions yourself, it is not fitting for me to listen to or behold you.
To come forward to meet me with such distress is but to increase my weariness and vexation in vain.
When the father heard his son’s words and saw that his resolve was firm, he was struck dumb with uncertainty; filled with shame and remorse, he had no words with which to respond.
The king said:

“Just as when you were a king in a previous life, you practiced all manner of virtues; yet for even a minor transgression, though it is not something you can recall, you still suffered such punishment and hardship.”

Now, in governing my kingdom, I do not uphold the True Dharma; having no subtle merit whatsoever, I instead pursue what is contrary and wrong, acting with arrogance, pride, and self-indulgence, practicing nothing but perilous deeds. What price shall I pay for such transgressions?
He then released the Prince, permitting him to go forth and study the Way.

Thereupon, the Prince abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royal status; he no longer sought after worldly things, but focused his mind with single-minded devotion, contemplating the Way and cultivating virtue. As his merits accumulated, he eventually attained Buddhahood.

The Buddha, having already attained the Way, further delivered the devas and people of the ten directions—countless and beyond measure—for incalculable kalpas without ever regarding it as wearisome; such was the diligent suffering endured by the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"At that time, the prince was I myself;
the father-king was my present father, Śuddhodana."
The mother was Māyā;
the Brahmin physiognomist at that time was Devadatta;
and the servants were the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
All those who take the Way as their goal should respectfully follow the Buddha’s teachings and not violate the sutras or the precepts;
though practicing the Way is difficult, it is superior to being in the three evil realms or the eight states of hardship.

Violating the precepts and transgressing prohibitions leads to falling into the evil realms in the future; even if one attains liberation to become human again, one will be born into poverty and suffering, or become a slave, with no freedom of will.
By upholding the precepts and practicing goodness, the Three Honored Ones may be attained.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the assembly of bhikṣus, the devas, and the people were all filled with joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
This concludes the *Sūtra on Prince Mubao* as spoken by the Buddha.
